parts.text:
A remarkably strong El Niño has formed in the Pacific.

This natural phenomenon drives variations in temperature,

and winds across the globe. The ongoing El Niño has already contributed to sudden floods in eastern Africa, blistering heatwaves in Europe and intense hurricanes in the eastern Pacific.

Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology

us of this El Niño in June, which is currently the earliest point at which reliable predictions can be made.

Our new study suggests it may be possible to accurately predict some El Niños up to 12 months ahead of time, buying valuable time for farmers,

services and disaster-prone communities.

How models predict El Niño and La Niña

Climate and weather forecasting largely relies on physics-based models of the Earth’s atmosphere and oceans. These models work by applying the laws of physics, such as Newton’s laws of

, to Earth’s geography.

A model is given information like the shapes of continents, the locations of mountains and the speed of Earth’s rotation. The models then solve equations representing the laws of physics to

a version of our Earth, complete with its own storms, ocean currents, waves and wind patterns.

To make predictions of El Niños and La Niñas, forecasters supply these models with information about present conditions, including ocean temperatures, currents, winds and
. This data comes from a vast global network of satellites, weather stations, ocean buoys and

.

The models use this information about the present as a starting point. They then simulate the ocean and atmosphere’s movements and temperatures a few months into the future, showing whether an El Niño or La Niña is about to emerge.

Why is it difficult to make early forecasts?

In the 1960s,

Ed Lorenz and computer scientist Margaret Hamilton made a startling discovery. Using an early weather model, they found changing the starting conditions by a tiny amount, such as a millionth of a degree Celsius, could radically alter the model’s predictions.

This

the mathematical field of chaos theory, the idea that no matter how perfect a model is, there are some situations where the system being predicted is so sensitive to minuscule changes, it’s almost impossible to make
predictions. This makes it extremely difficult to form accurate forecasts of weather more than a week or two in advance.
